answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: First, the crisis destroyed faith in collective security: sanctions had been tried and failed, so small states knew the League could not protect them. Second, it pushed Mussolini towards Hitler, leading to the Rome-Berlin Axis in 1936 and Italy's departure from the League in 1937, while Hitler used the distraction to remilitarise the Rhineland in March 1936.

> A large, armed figure in a black shirt, labelled "Italy", strides over a map of East Africa. answerSpec.modelAnswer: The failure to ban oil was important, as the cartoon shows: Italy's tanks, lorries and aircraft depended on oil, so without an oil ban the sanctions could not stop the war. However, other factors were just as important. Britain did not close the Suez Canal, so Italian supplies kept flowing. Britain and France wanted Italy as an ally against Hitler after the Stresa Front, and the Hoare-Laval Pact showed they were ready to reward Mussolini. The USA, a major oil supplier, was not a member, and the war lasted only seven months, so sanctions had little time to bite. Overall the oil decision was a symptom of a deeper problem: Britain and France were not willing to risk war to stop Mussolini.

hints: Look at the size of the figures and the oil barrel.

parts.stem: "The Abyssinian crisis did more damage to the League than the Manchurian crisis." How far do you agree?

points.description: Abyssinia: sanctions tried and failed, exposing the League's main weapon.
Abyssinia: Hoare-Laval showed the leading members betraying the Covenant; close to Europe; drove Italy to Hitler.
Manchuria: first case of a great power getting away with aggression; no sanctions at all; set a precedent.
Manchuria: Japan left; showed slowness (a year to report); encouraged later aggressors.
Distance/context: Manchuria could be excused as far away; Abyssinia could not.
Supported judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Abyssinian crisis was arguably more damaging. Here the League did impose sanctions, so when they failed its main weapon was exposed as useless. The sanctions excluded oil, the Suez Canal stayed open, and the leaked Hoare-Laval Pact showed Britain and France secretly offering the aggressor much of Abyssinia. The crisis was close to Europe and involved a League member attacking another, so there was no excuse. It also drove Mussolini towards Hitler and distracted attention while Hitler remilitarised the Rhineland.

On the other hand, Manchuria came first and set the precedent. A great power seized territory from another member and suffered nothing but criticism; the League took a year to report and imposed no sanctions at all. Japan simply left. Mussolini and Hitler could see that aggression worked.

Overall Manchuria showed the League's weakness, but it could be excused because it was far away and Britain and France had no forces there. Abyssinia destroyed the League's credibility completely, because it failed even when it tried to act, so I largely agree with the statement.

parts.explanation: Both sides and a supported judgement.

hints: In (b), compare the two crises on several criteria.
